slides.title: ID3 learns a tree that describes class patterns
slides.visibleText:
DECISION-TREE CONCEPT
Decision tree induction
Quinlan developed ID3 in 1986
a tree represents concepts through property tests
labeled training data induce classification rules
PROVENANCE

J. Ross Quinlan developed ID3 in 1986 as an early decision-tree learning algorithm.

REPRESENTATION

A decision tree represents conditional patterns or concepts as a graph of tests and outcomes.

LEARNING

ID3 uses labeled input data to induce a tree—and therefore a set of classification rules.

slides.title: ID3 recursively turns impure partitions into subtrees
slides.visibleText:
DECISION-TREE CONCEPT
ID3 recursive algorithm
if all examples share a class, return a leaf
if no attributes remain, return a default class
otherwise select a test, partition, and recurse
BASE CASE A

All examples have one class → return that class.

BASE CASE B

No attributes remain → return a default or majority class.

RECURSIVE CASE

Select a test, partition the examples, and induce one subtree per non-pure branch.

READ THE SOURCE AS CODE
Circle the stopping conditions. Underline the line that makes the algorithm greedy.

slides.title: If several trees fit the data, which one should we prefer?
slides.visibleText:
DECISION-TREE VISUAL
Choosing among consistent trees
income?
$0–$15k → high
$15–$35k → credit / debt
>$35k → credit
Collateral is never selected in the learned tree.
many trees may fit the training data · prefer a compact pattern, then verify generalization
Prefer a tree that captures the pattern without merely memorizing the records.
SMALLER TREE
lower description cost

often easier to inspect and less likely to encode accidental detail

BUT VERIFY
validation performance

the shortest tree is not automatically the most accurate or fair

IN-CLASS QUESTION
Give one reason a larger tree might fit training data better yet predict new applications worse.

slides.title: A useful pattern compresses the data it explains
slides.visibleText:
DECISION-TREE CONCEPT
Minimum message length
minimize description of the hypothesis plus data given the hypothesis
the integers 2–100 contain 50 even values
Choose Hᵢ minimizing Mlength(Hᵢ) + Mlength(D | Hᵢ)
MODEL COST

bits needed to specify the hypothesis

RESIDUAL COST

bits needed to describe the data given the hypothesis

SOURCE CORRECTION
The even integers from 2 through 100 inclusive number 50, not 49. The compression argument still holds: “all even integers from 2 to 100” is shorter than listing all 50 integers.

slides.title: Entropy measures uncertainty in a class distribution
slides.visibleText:
DECISION-TREE CONCEPT
Entropy and information
I(c)=−log₂p(c)
H(S)=−Σp(c)log₂p(c)
pure sets have entropy 0
I(c) = −log₂ p(c)
H(S) = −Σ p(c) log₂ p(c)
H = 0

one class only; no uncertainty

H is high

classes are balanced; the label is uncertain

INTERPRETATION
Entropy is about the distribution of labels in a set—not the visual complexity of a tree.

slides.title: Choose the test that removes the most expected uncertainty
slides.visibleText:
DECISION-TREE CONCEPT
Information gain
E(X)=Σᵥ |Tᵥ|/|T| · H(Tᵥ)
Gain(X)=H(T)−E(X)
choose the largest gain
E(X) = Σᵥ |Tᵥ| / |T| · H(Tᵥ)
Gain(X) = H(T) − E(X)
1
Measure uncertainty before the split.
2
Compute each branch's entropy.
3
Weight branches by their sizes.
4
Subtract expected uncertainty from the parent entropy.
DECISION RULE
ID3 chooses the candidate attribute with the largest information gain.

Loan-data calculation
H(LoanData)=1.531 bits
E(income)=0.564 bits
Gain(income)=0.967 bits
income has the largest gain
H(LoanData) = −6/14 log₂(6/14) − 3/14 log₂(3/14) − 5/14 log₂(5/14) = 1.531
E(income) = 4/14(0) + 4/14(1) + 6/14(0.65) = 0.564
Gain(income) = 1.531 − 0.564 = 0.967 bits

Other gains: credit history 0.266 · collateral 0.206 · debt 0.063. Therefore income becomes the root.

Tests on one path are joined by AND. Multiple paths to the same class are joined by OR.

slides.title: ID3 greedily searches a concept space of possible trees
slides.visibleText:
DECISION-TREE CONCEPT
Decision-tree induction as search
state: partially built tree
operator: add an attribute test
heuristic: information gain
greedy search uses no backtracking
STATE
a partially built tree
SPACE
all trees constructible from the examples
OPERATOR
add an attribute test
HEURISTIC
choose maximum information gain
CONSEQUENCE
Greedy and no backtracking makes ID3 efficient, but the locally best split need not produce the globally smallest or best-generalizing tree.

categorical target

risk ∈ high, moderate, low; evaluate class errors and probabilities

numeric target

predict expected loss or dollar amount; evaluate residual magnitude

OVERFITTING
training detail becomes brittle rules

deep branches can fit noise, rare cases, or mislabeled records

PRUNING
remove unsupported complexity

pre-prune with stopping rules or post-prune using validation evidence

MODEL-SELECTION DISCIPLINE
Fit the tree on training data, choose depth or pruning on validation data, and report the untouched test set once.

slides.title: One score is not enough evidence for deployment
slides.visibleText:
EVALUATION LENS
ROC vs PR

ROC compares TPR and FPR; PR is often more revealing when the positive class is rare.

Calibration

Among predictions near 0.7, roughly 70% should occur if probabilities are calibrated.

Subgroups

Report error, recall, calibration, and sample size for relevant groups—not only the aggregate.
